events.description: An engineer starts setting up multiple PostgreSQL servers in the staging environment to try out pgpool-II for load balancing queries (infrastructure#259).
Prior to starting the work, the engineer takes an LVM snapshot of the production database and loads it into the staging environment to get a more up-to-date copy than the automatic daily one.

GitLab.com starts experiencing an increase in database load, suspected to be spam; many users are unable to post comments on issues and merge requests, and getting load under control takes several hours.

Due to increased load, the PostgreSQL secondary's replication lags and fails because WAL segments were already removed from the primary; the secondary must be re-synchronised manually via pg_basebackup, which hangs, and max_wal_senders is raised from 3 to 32, then max_connections is reduced from 8000 to 2000 so PostgreSQL can restart.

An engineer suspects pg_basebackup created files in the secondary's data directory during earlier attempts; while trying to restore replication, an engineer errantly wipes the PostgreSQL data directory on the primary instead of the secondary, removing around 300 GB of data before the process is terminated a second or two later.

Engineers look for database backups and discover the pg_dump backups were never created: the procedure used pg_dump 9.2 against PostgreSQL 9.6, failing silently since DMARC rejected the failure notification emails, and the S3 bucket is empty.
A snapshot is manually created by an engineer, one of only two LVM snapshots available for recovery.
The GitLab.com database is restored without webhooks, using the LVM snapshot taken at January 31st 17:20 UTC after roughly 18 hours of copying data between staging and production.
Final restoration procedures, including restoring webhooks and confirming operation, are completed.
